messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Method | Type | Published accuracy metrics | Strengths | Weaknesses | Suitability for dense spherical metal powders |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Otsu or global thresholding | Classical semantic segmentation | No metal-powder instance-segmentation benchmark identified in the cited evidence. | Fast, reproducible, parameter-light; effective with uniform BSE compositional contrast, where metal is bright against carbon tape. | Produces connected foreground rather than particle instances; sensitive to SE shading, charging, carbon-tape texture, and intensity gradients; cannot resolve overlap alone. | **Useful preprocessing only.** Prefer BSE over SE, then apply marker-controlled watershed or another instance method. BSE threshold segmentation of powder on carbon tape has been demonstrated using strong atomic-number contrast (pqac-00000059). |
| Local or adaptive thresholding | Classical semantic segmentation | No powder-specific precision/recall benchmark identified. | Handles illumination gradients, edge darkening, and particle-to-particle brightness differences better than a single global threshold. | Window size can erase fines or create false foreground inside shaded coarse particles; still merges touching particles and may interpret surface texture as boundaries. | **Useful preprocessing when BSE intensity is nonuniform.** Validate window size by particle-size class; not adequate as the final instance segmentation. |
| Distance-transform, marker-controlled watershed | Classical instance segmentation | On 50 metal-powder SEM images: **99.3% precision, 89.2% recall**; lower recall was attributed to failure on heavily overlapping particles (pqac-00000005). | Transparent, inexpensive, reproducible; well matched to isolated or lightly touching near-circular particles; markers can be tuned with h-maxima or minimum peak distance. | Too many markers cause over-segmentation; suppressed markers cause merging; distance peaks disappear under strong overlap, satellites, irregular particles, and broad size distributions. | **Good baseline, but insufficient alone for the present dense fields.** Tune markers by scale and audit split/merge errors separately. |
| Circular Hough transform (CHT) | Classical model-based detection | On the same metal-powder benchmark: **95.2% precision, 93.8% recall**; runtime 0.688 s per image (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). | Can infer circular particles despite partial overlap or incomplete visible arcs; directly returns center and radius. | Broad radius searches generate duplicate and overlapping false circles; vulnerable to noisy edges, satellites, irregular particles, and internal SE texture; imposes circularity and does not yield a trustworthy measured contour. | **Poor as a full-field detector for these images**, consistent with the reported thousands of false circles. It may be useful only after candidate-region segmentation and strict non-maximum suppression. |
| Region segmentation followed by local CHT, Li et al. (2023) | Classical hybrid instance detection | Across 50 SEM images of Ni₃Al, TC4, and TiAl powders: **99.3% precision, 99.5% recall** and 0.136 s per image, versus watershed 99.3%/89.2% and direct CHT 95.2%/93.8% (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). | Restricts circle fitting to individual candidate regions, sharply reducing false circles and computation; handles substantial overlap and broad size ranges; metal-powder-specific evidence. | Accuracy concerns particle identification rather than mask-boundary fidelity; circle fitting can hide satellites or irregularity and bias projected area, perimeter, and shape descriptors. | **Strong candidate for spherical-particle counting and diameter**, but retain contour-based masks for morphology and manually audit irregular, satellite-bearing, and occluded particles. |
| Mask R-CNN, Yichao et al. (2021) | Supervised deep-learning instance segmentation | Metal-powder study reported **23.6% higher recognition accuracy** than traditional segmentation; 12,192 particles were identified in eight images. Training used 100 subimages containing 14,835 labels, but precision, recall, IoU, and AP were not reported (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). | Designed for individual instances; recognizes touching, overlapping, partially occluded, nonspherical, and satellite particles; directly produces masks and classes. | Requires representative annotations and retraining for a new alloy, detector, magnification, and preparation; inferred hidden boundaries may be model-dependent; the published metric is incompletely specified. | **Promising and metal-powder-specific**, especially after fine-tuning on Apreo BSE/SE images. Do not accept pretrained output without local held-out validation. |
| Uncertainty-aware Mask R-CNN, Rettenberger et al. (2024) | Supervised deep-learning instance segmentation | On held-out inorganic-powder SEM images, mean **AJI+ was 0.81 versus 0.55 for U-Net at low magnification**, and **0.51 versus 0.34 at high magnification**; Mask R-CNN won on 14 of 15 test images (pqac-00000027). | Handles overlapping, clustered, irregular, blurry, and differently sized particles; uncertainty score supports manual review; approximately 3 min automated analysis versus 145–430 min for experts (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000030). | Performance falls at difficult high magnification; expert labels themselves disagreed; transfer across imaging regimes is not guaranteed, and separate models were needed for low and high magnification. | **Best-supported DL architecture for difficult powder SEM among the cited studies.** Fine-tune locally and route low-confidence masks to manual correction. |
| BPartIS | Bayesian deep-learning instance segmentation | Evaluated on the 465-image EMPS dataset using AP, AP50, AP75, and mean IoU; uncertainty filtering improved performance over conventional image processing, Gaussian-mixture labeling, and Mask R-CNN, but numerical AP values were not available in the cited excerpt. Distribution errors included cosine distances of 0.02111 for size and 0.03261 for aspect ratio (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000029). | Provides instance masks plus epistemic uncertainty; filters false positives from scale bars and background texture; supports quantitative size and aspect-ratio distributions. | General electron-microscopy dataset rather than a dedicated atomized-metal-powder benchmark; substantial overlaps can remain challenging; requires model deployment and domain validation. | **Good validation-oriented option**, particularly where uncertainty-based review is valuable; fine-tune and compare against powder-specific Mask R-CNN and watershed baselines. |
| Cellpose | Pretrained or fine-tuned flow-based deep-learning instance segmentation | No published atomized-metal-powder SEM benchmark or precision/recall comparison was identified in the cited evidence. | Easy interactive use; flow representation often separates touching rounded objects; supports retraining from corrected masks. | Generic pretrained models are predominantly biological; may merge heavily overlapped particles, mistake SE highlights for boundaries, or smooth away satellites; diameter parameter is scale-sensitive. | **Exploratory baseline only.** Fine-tune on locally annotated powder images and require held-out mask-IoU, split/merge, size-bias, and shape-bias validation before quantitative use. |
| StarDist | Supervised star-convex deep-learning instance segmentation | No atomized-metal-powder SEM benchmark was identified in the cited evidence. | Star-convex representation is naturally suited to isolated spherical or mildly overlapping particles; efficient instance separation and non-maximum suppression. | Strongly concave agglomerates, satellite-bearing particles, and irregular shapes violate the star-convex assumption; inferred contours can suppress real morphology. | **Potentially strong for primary spherical particles**, but use separate labels for satellites/agglomerates and validate contour-derived shape descriptors rather than detection alone. |
| SAM or micro-SAM | Foundation-model-assisted instance segmentation | No published quantitative benchmark on dense atomized-metal-powder SEM images was identified in the cited evidence. | Rapid interactive annotation; useful for building a training set and correcting masks; micro-SAM adds microscopy-oriented tiling, embeddings, and tracking tools. | Zero-shot masks are prompt- and contrast-dependent; adjacent similar particles may merge, while textured surfaces may fragment; no intrinsic guarantee of metrological boundary accuracy or consistent hidden-boundary reconstruction. | **Best used as an annotation accelerator, not the final metrology method.** Fine-tune or use curated prompts, then validate against independent expert masks and hand-measured diameters. |


*Table: Comparison of classical and deep-learning methods for separating touching and overlapping spherical particles in SEM images, including published metal-powder metrics and explicit evidence gaps for generic pretrained models.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a summary table of key standards and their requirements/recommendations for image-based particle sizing of metal powders for additive manufacturing. Include: ISO 13322-1 (static image analysis), ISO 9276-1 (representation), ISO 9276-2 (moments, weighting conversion), ISO 9276-6 (shape descriptors, 100-5000 pixels/particle), ISO 14488 (sample splitting), ASTM F3049 (AM powder characterization guide), ASTM B822 (laser diffraction), ASTM B214 (sieve analysis), ASTM F3571 (morphology classification). For each, include columns: Standard, Scope, Key requirements/recommendations for image analysis, and Relevance to user's SEM analysis. Based on evidence gathered."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Standard | Scope | Key requirements/recommendations for image analysis | Relevance to the user’s SEM analysis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISO 13322-1:2014** | Static image analysis for particle-size distributions | Define the measured size explicitly—normally projected-area-equivalent diameter, with Feret dimensions where shape or orientation matters. Use representative sampling and dispersion, calibrated image scale, adequate resolution and particle count, documented segmentation and border rules, and report distribution basis, size classes, instrument, preparation, calibration and analysis procedure. Particle count depends on distribution width and required uncertainty rather than one universal minimum (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000015). | This is the governing image-analysis standard. Nine crowded fields from one sprinkled stub do not establish an ISO-conforming lot PSD unless representativeness, traceable calibration, counting precision, segmentation validity and treatment of touching or occluded particles are demonstrated. |
| **ISO 9276-1** | Representation of particle-size-analysis results | Establishes notation and presentation of differential and cumulative distributions, size classes and weighting basis. Reports must identify whether results are number-, length-, area-, volume- or mass-weighted; percentiles with different weighting bases are not directly equivalent. | Report separate cumulative **Q0** and model-derived **Q3** curves, D10/D50/D90 and span. Do not describe a number-weighted SEM percentile as equivalent to a laser-diffraction percentile without conversion and qualification. |
| **ISO 9276-2** | Calculation of mean sizes, moments and conversion between distribution bases | Uses distribution moments to convert weighting orders. For equal-density equivalent spheres, number-to-volume conversion weights each particle by diameter cubed. State the conversion and assumed size and shape model; transformed results are highly sensitive to rare large particles and size truncation (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000017). | Calculate Q3 from projected-area-equivalent diameters only as a model-derived equivalent-sphere distribution. Retain Q0 as the primary image result and bootstrap the complete conversion because a few 200–260 µm particles can dominate Q3 and D90. |
| **ISO 9276-6** | Quantitative description of particle shape and morphology | Define every descriptor and formula. Relevant quantities include perimeter-based circularity, aspect or ellipse ratio, convexity and solidity. Cited implementation guidance represents each particle with approximately **100–5000 pixels**. Perimeter and circularity vary with resolution and perimeter algorithm, so pixel size, threshold and estimator must be fixed and reported (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022). | At 0.67–1.01 µm/px, a 10 µm particle contains only about 77–175 projected pixels: marginal for size and inadequate for defensible perimeter or satellite morphology. Acquire higher-magnification fields for fines and shape, and state the exact circularity formula. |
| **ISO 14488** | Sampling and sample splitting of particulate materials | Obtain representative laboratory and test portions through documented splitting and repeated subdivision; avoid scoop or surface sampling that permits size segregation. Record lot identity, sampling location, splitting device, split sequence, test-portion mass and replicate portions. | Split the bulk atomized lot before stub preparation, preferably using a rotary divider or validated riffler. Prepare independent stubs from independent final splits; one conveniently selected portion on one stub does not establish lot representativeness. |
| **ASTM F3049** | Guide to characterization of metal powders used in powder-based AM | This is a guide rather than a stand-alone image-analysis method. It identifies relevant powder properties and directs users to established methods for PSD, morphology, chemistry, density and flow. The material condition—virgin, used, blended or recycled—and the applied methods should be identified (pqac-00000038). | Use it to define the qualification package: ISO 13322-1 image analysis for size and morphology, ASTM B822 laser diffraction and ASTM B214 sieving as complementary PSD methods, plus chemistry, density and flow tests appropriate to DED. |
| **ASTM B822** | Particle-size distribution of metal powders by light scattering or laser diffraction | Requires representative sampling and controlled dry or wet dispersion, instrument checks, suitable obscuration, repeat measurements, specified optical assumptions and reporting of preparation, dispersion conditions, instrument and volume-based PSD. Results are sensitive to agglomeration, orientation and optical settings (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000033). | Recommended as an independent Q3 reference for unsieved powder. Differences from SEM Q0 and SEM-derived Q3 are expected, especially below 20 µm and for satellites or agglomerates; keep dispersion conditions constant for lot comparisons. |
| **ASTM B214** | Sieve analysis of metal powders | Uses a representative test portion, specified and verified sieve series, controlled mechanical sieving, weighing of retained fractions and a mass-balance check. Results are mass fractions bounded by sieve apertures, not projected-image diameters. | This is the primary process-control method for confirming the intended **50–200 µm DED cut** and quantifying undersize and oversize after sieving. It cannot characterize detailed morphology, satellites or the continuous distribution within the cut. |
| **ASTM F3571** | Quantitative characterization of metal-powder morphology by image analysis | Recommends explicit descriptor definitions and use of multiple descriptors. Aspect or ellipse ratio combined with solidity is useful for separating spherical and nonspherical particles. Resolution, thresholding and software algorithms must be controlled because one descriptor alone can classify unlike shapes similarly (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). | Use with ISO 9276-6 to predefine spherical, elongated, irregular, satellite-bearing and agglomerated classes. Derive classification thresholds from manually labelled C63000 particles rather than importing thresholds from another alloy or software package. |


*Table: Summary of the principal ISO and ASTM standards governing representative sampling, static image analysis, distribution weighting, morphology, laser diffraction and sieving. It distinguishes requirements applicable to the SEM workflow from complementary methods used to qualify the 50–200 µm DED cut.*

Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We ultrasonically atomized a nickel-aluminium bronze (UNS C63000, Cu-10Al-5Ni-4Fe) on an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER and want a particle size and shape distribution from SEM images, done to best
practice, before sieving to a directed-energy-deposition cut of 50-200 um. The powder is mostly
spherical, from <10 um fines to ~260 um, with satellites and a few irregular or agglomerated
particles. It was sprinkled on carbon tape on one stub and imaged in a Thermo Fisher Apreo C with the
secondary-electron (ETD) detector: nine usable 3072 x 2048 px fields at 133-200x (0.67-1.01 um per
pixel), densely packed, with many touching and overlapping particles. A naive Hough-circle detection
returned thousands of overlapping false circles per field. We plan distance-transform watershed
segmentation and are weighing pretrained models (Cellpose, StarDist, Segment Anything / SAM, and
SEM-powder-specific deep-learning models), and we have a few hand measurements to validate against.

Please give the best-practice method, with numbers and sources, for:

1. Standards. What ISO 13322-1 (static image analysis), ISO 9276-1, -2 and -6 (representation of
   results, moments, and shape descriptors), ISO 14488 (sample splitting), ASTM F3049 (characterizing
   powders for AM), ASTM B822 (laser diffraction for metal powders) and ASTM B214 (sieve analysis)
   require or recommend for image-based particle sizing: the size measure (projected-area equivalent
   circle diameter vs Feret diameters), magnification and pixel requirements, minimum particle
   counts, calibration and traceability (stage micrometer / certified reference beads), and what a
   report must state.

2. Counting statistics. The minimum number of particles for D10, D50 and D90 by number and by volume
   at a stated precision (e.g. the ISO 13322-1 / Masuda-Gotoh style estimate of the count needed for
   a given relative error in a volume-weighted percentile, and the ~10,000-particle figures quoted for
   robust morphology). How should confidence intervals on percentiles be computed (bootstrap,
   order-statistic, Masuda-Gotoh), and why does the volume-weighted D90 need far more particles than
   the number-weighted D50?

3. Pixel resolution. The minimum number of pixels across (or pixel area of) the smallest particle
   for reliable size, and separately for reliable shape (circularity, aspect ratio, solidity), with
   quantitative estimates of the bias in circularity and perimeter for small, pixelated objects, and
   how perimeter estimators (Crofton, chain-code corrections) reduce it. What lower size cut-off
   should be applied for a given pixel size?

4. Segmentation of touching and overlapping spherical particles: thresholding (Otsu, local/adaptive),
   distance-transform marker-controlled watershed (h-maxima marker selection, over- and
   under-segmentation), ellipse/circle fitting on contours, Cellpose, StarDist, SAM / micro-SAM and
   powder-specific CNNs (e.g. Mask R-CNN models trained on AM-powder SEM images). Report published
   accuracy comparisons on metal powders or similar dense spherical particles (precision/recall, size
   bias versus manual measurement), and what validation is considered adequate.

5. Edge effects. Exclusion of particles that touch the image frame and the standard bias correction
   (Miles-Lantuejoul guard-frame weighting, w = (W*H)/((W - d)(H - d)) for a particle of extent d), and
   how it is reported. Also: double counting in overlapping fields, and how to handle partially
   hidden (occluded) particles in multilayer fields.

6. Number- to volume-weighted conversion. Converting a number distribution of projected-area

The toluene insolubles (TI) was recognized as coking precursors produced at the initial stage of thermal reaction. The traditional methods can only obtain the overall yield of TI, however, more detailed information, such as the size distribution, and the shape parameters of TI, cannot be provided. Abstract:
In the European Union, nanomaterials are regulated through different pieces of sectoral legislation. This legislation often requires risk assessments and thus reliable characterization data, for which regulatory guidance generally recommend electron microscopy. The guidance provides best practices for measurements but lacks requirements on how many particles to measure. Using transmission electron microscopy data of nanomaterials, a strategy based on repeated subsampling is proposed to establish, for different particle size and shape measurands, mathematical relationships between particle count and precision, and subsequently to determine the minimum particle count. Our results confirm that the minimum particle count generally depends on the width of the size and shape distributions and that the median of the distribution can be determined with the highest precision compared to other percentiles. Upon combining the precision uncertainty related to particle number with uncertainties from other sources, such as sample preparation, calibration and trueness, we reach an optimal particle count above which additional particle measurements only yield negligible improvements to the combined measurement uncertainty. Our findings offer an experimental approach for determining the minimum particle count to measure particle size and shape by electron microscopy. It enables efficient analyses and facilitates compliance with legislation addressing nanomaterials across various application domains.                   <jats:p>Porous 430L stainless steel metal supports fabricated by direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) with various designed pore sizes were evaluated for solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) applications. This study reports the metal support properties related to pore size and surface roughness that are critical for defect-free ceramic deposition. The supports were systematically characterized in terms of pore size fidelity and printability, surface pore distribution and roughness, and bridging layer deposition and adhesion relevant to SOFC fabrication and operation. Challenges associated with conventional pore former usage and pore size control were mitigated by designing and printing fine and straight-through pores, while overall porosity was custom-designed and optimized within the printability limit of the DMLS process. Pore size and surface pore distribution were quantified using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) micrographs and image processing techniques. Surface roughness was evaluated using an optical profilometer on bare, polished, gadolinium-doped ceria-coated, and yttria-stabilized zirconia-coated samples. The observed adhesion of the ceramic layers and the improved surface smoothness indicated good compatibility between the additively manufactured metal supports and ceramic coatings, supporting their potential for SOFC applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal foams offer attractive properties for lightweight structures. This study presents the development of a powder metallurgical aluminum alloy intended for foamable wires that can be used in additive manufacturing processes such as wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Unlike established aluminum wrought alloys, whose melting range is not well suited for foaming, or cast alloys which are not easily extruded into thin wires, the custom AlMg2Si1.2 alloy developed in this study combines a melting interval matched to the decomposition of pre-oxidized blowing agent (TiH
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) with a low alloying content suitable for high extrusion ratios. For this, the alloy composition was determined using thermodynamic calculations. The material was then cast into billets, which were extruded into rod electrodes. Pre-alloyed metal powder was produced from these electrodes using electrode induction melting inert gas atomization (EIGA), and the influence of atomization gas parameters on powder properties was investigated. Increasing the gas pressure from 16.8 bar to 23.0 bar reduced the median particle size from 51 to 40 µm. The best flowability was observed for the fraction 63–90 µm. A solidus temperature of 560 °C and a liquidus of 646 °C were determined by differential scanning calorimetry, aligning with the principal hydrogen-release peak of the blowing agent. Foam samples produced from the powder confirmed the material’s foamability, reaching porosities of 64–68%, as determined by X-ray microscopy. These results indicate that AlMg2Si1.2 processed via EIGA yields reproducible, highly porous foams, and is a suitable basis for foamable wires in WAAM.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Recovered metallic waste can be used in additive manufacturing as a feedstock if the subsequent steps of the waste-to-product process are sufficiently mastered. In this study, impact of recycling of Z100 duplex steel mixed with 316L steel on the resulting powders microstructure and chemical composition was investigated. The utility of the original method of recycling stainless steels into a high-grade powder suitable for additive techniques has been demonstrated. By examining three gradations of powders, namely 20–50 μm, 50–100 μm and 125–250 μm, differences in selected properties in relation to the average particle size are shown. The results suggest that with increasing the particle diameter, fine-crystalline γ-austenite is favoured to precipitate at the boundaries and within the volume of the originally formed large δ-ferrite grains. It is reflected by a decrease of δ/γ fraction ratio from 0.64 in the 20–50 μm powders to 0.20 in the 125–250 μm, respectively. Obtained results indicate non-diffusional, shear or semi-shear character of δ → γ + δ phase transformation. The resulting fine-crystalline austenite is characterised by a significant dislocation density, which induces dislocation strengthening effect, responsible for an increase in Vickers hardness from 145 HV and Young's modulus from 29 GPa in the 20–50 μm group to 310 HV and 146 GPa in the 125–250 μm fraction, respectively.

Abstract:
Automated particle segmentation and feature analysis of experimental image data are indispensable for data-driven material science. Deep learning-based image segmentation algorithms are promising techniques to achieve this goal but are challenging to use due to the acquisition of a large number of training images. In the present work, synthetic images are applied, resembling the experimental images in terms of geometrical and visual features, to train the state-of-art Mask region-based convolutional neural networks to segment vanadium pentoxide nanowires, a cathode material within optical density-based images acquired using spectromicroscopy. The results demonstrate the instance segmentation power in real optical intensity-based spectromicroscopy images of complex nanowires in overlapped networks and provide reliable statistical information. The model can further be used to segment nanowires in scanning electron microscopy images, which are fundamentally different from the training dataset known to the model. The proposed methodology can be extended to any optical intensity-based images of variable particle morphology, material class, and beyond.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The intersection of deep learning (DL) and materials electron microscopy (EM) has significantly expanded since the early 2010 s; however, the diversity of model architectures and use cases makes it hard to identify literature gaps and determine which models are well-established in this field of application. This work provides a model-centric overview of DL applied to EM, with special focus on transmission EM, organized around three functional branches: representation (convolutional neural networks, residual networks, U-Net variants, and transformer-based architectures), analysis (object detectors such as Mask R-CNN and YOLO), and generation (variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and denoising diffusion probabilistic models). The evolution of these model families is traced from AlexNet (2012) through ResNets and U-Nets (2015), vision transformers (2020–2021), and current hybrid architectures, with a characteristic lag of three to seven years between model conception and first application in materials science. A bibliographic analysis of more than 1 800 peer-reviewed articles, collected from the Web of Science and classified using an LLM-augmented regex methodology, provides co-occurrence matrices and publication trends that offer a quantitative context for these developments. The results indicate that U-Net and generic CNN variants dominate the current literature, while transformer-based and generative models remain underrepresented. The article also compiles a broad collection of DL applications in materials microscopy, examined through the lens of materials scientists, and discusses the specific challenges and perspectives that emerge, including standardized benchmark datasets, foundation models, and multimodal data fusion.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Automating the analysis portion of materials characterization by electron microscopy (EM) has the potential to accelerate the process of scientific discovery. To this end, we present a Bayesian deep-learning model for semantic segmentation and localization of particle instances in EM images. These segmentations can subsequently be used to compute quantitative measures such as particle-size distributions, radial- distribution functions, average sizes, and aspect ratios of the particles in an image. Moreover, by making use of the epistemic uncertainty of our model, we obtain uncertainty estimates of its outputs and use these to filter out false-positive predictions and hence produce more accurate quantitative measures. We incorporate our method into the ImageDataExtractor package, as ImageDataExtractor 2.0, which affords a full pipeline to automatically extract particle information for large-scale data-driven materials discovery. Finally, we present and make publicly available the Electron Microscopy Particle Segmentation (EMPS) data set. This is the first human-labeled particle instance segmentation data set, consisting of 465 EM images and their corresponding semantic instance segmentation maps.

Abstract:
The spreading of powders into thin layers is a critical step in powder bed additive manufacturing, but there is no accepted technique to test it. There is not even a metric that can be used to describe spreading behaviour. A robust, image-based measurement procedure has been developed and can be implemented at modest cost and with minimal training. The analysis is automated to derive quantitative information about the characteristics of the spread layer. The technique has been demonstrated for three powders to quantify their spreading behaviour as a function of layer thickness and spreading speed. Abstract:
The quality of powder used in powder bed-based additive manufacturing plays a key role concerning process performance and end part properties. Even though this is a generally accepted fact, there is still a lack of a comprehensive understanding of the powder property–part property relationship. However, numerous investigations focusing on selected powder properties and their corresponding influence on process aspects or final part properties have been published in recent years. Still, generalized statements on powder requirements for a defined process performance are not available. This can be attributed to the fact that the community has not yet come to an agreement which characterization techniques are most suitable for powder characterization in the additive manufacturing context and in most cases only selected aspects have been investigated for special powder materials. The aim of this review is to assess these building blocks of knowledge and to provide an overview on the current state of the art.

Abstract:
Characterizing powder feedstock is crucial for ensuring the quality and reliability of parts produced through metal additive manufacturing (AM). The morphology of particles impacts the flowability, packing density, and spreadability of powders, affecting productivity and part quality. A new methodology has been developed to classify particle morphological features in AM powder feedstocks, such as spherical or elongated shapes, and the presence of satellites and facets. This approach uses multiple descriptors for quantitative evaluation. The results from shape descriptors can vary based on image resolution, gray/color thresholding, and software algorithms. There are various commercial systems available for characterizing particle shape, some of which use images taken of static particles, while others use images of particles in motion. This diversity can lead to differences in powder characterization across laboratories with different equipment and methods. This paper compares results from a particle classification approach using two software programs that work with metallographic images with those from an automated static particle analyzer. While traditional methods offer higher resolution and precision, this study shows that automated systems can achieve similar particle shape classification using different shape descriptors and thresholds.

Abstract:
Besides process parameters, powder properties such as grain size, morphology, and chemical composition have the highest impact on the material properties of parts produced by powder-based additive manufacturing. These properties are strongly influenced by the production process of the powder and its feedstock. In the scope of this work, the influence of three different powder producers of Ti6Al4V, on density, chemical composition, and mechanical properties of build samples, is investigated. Furthermore, the effects of the varying atomization process on morphology, particle size distribution, chemical composition, and oxide layers are studied. Particle size distribution and flowability seem to have a minor influence on the production process while density depends highly on the surface topology, sphericity, and nature of the oxide layer, which affect energy intake. Tensile properties are highly influenced by chemical composition, mainly dissolved oxygen, and polluting satellites, while notched bar impact strength is additionally influenced by the oxide layer and suspected TiO2 precipitations caused by it.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In recent years, Additive Manufacturing (AM), also called 3D printing, has been expanding into several industrial sectors due to the technology providing opportunities in terms of improved functionality, productivity, and competitiveness. While metal AM technologies have almost unlimited potential, and the range of applications has increased in recent years, industries have faced challenges in the adoption of these technologies and coping with a turbulent market. Despite the extensive work that has been completed on the properties of metal AM materials, there is still a need of a robust understanding of processes, challenges, application-specific needs, and considerations associated with these technologies. Therefore, the goal of this study is to present a comprehensive review of the most common metal AM technologies, an exploration of metal AM advancements, and industrial applications for the different AM technologies across various industry sectors. This study also outlines current limitations and challenges, which prevent industries to fully benefit from the metal AM opportunities, including production volume, standards compliance, post processing, product quality, maintenance, and materials range. Overall, this paper provides a survey as the benchmark for future industrial applications and research and development projects, in order to assist industries in selecting a suitable AM technology for their application.

Abstract:
The growing interest in the development of next-generation net zero energy systems has led to the expansion of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) research in this area. This activity has resulted in a wide range of manufacturing/synthesis methods, controllable morphologies, diverse carbonaceous composite structures, a multitude of applicable characterization techniques, and multiple energy applications for MoS2. To assess the literature trends, 37,347 MoS2 research articles from Web of Science were text scanned to classify articles according to energy application research and characterization techniques employed. Within the review, characterization techniques are grouped under the following categories: morphology, crystal structure, composition, and chemistry. The most common characterization techniques identified through text scanning are recommended as the base fingerprint for MoS2 samples. These include: scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and Raman spectroscopy. Similarly, XPS and Raman spectroscopy are suggested for 2H or 1T MoS2 phase confirmation. We provide guidance on the collection and presentation of MoS2 characterization data. This includes how to effectively combine multiple characterization techniques, considering the sample area probed by each technique and their statistical significance, and the benefit of using reference samples. For ease of access for future experimental comparison, key numeric MoS2 characterization values are tabulated and major literature discrepancies or currently debated characterization disputes are highlighted.

Abstract:
For polymer-based controlled release drug products (e.g. microspheres and implants), active pharmaceutical ingredient distribution and microporosity inside the polymer matrix are critical for product performance, particularly drug release kinetics. Due to the decreasing domain size and increasing complexity of such products, conventional characterization and release test techniques are limited by their resolution and speed. In this study, samples of controlled release poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) microspheres in the diameter range of 30–80 μm are investigated with focused ion beam scanning electron microscope imaging at 20 nm or higher resolution. Image data is quantified with artificial intelligence-based image analytics to provide size distributions of drug particles and pores within the microsphere sample. With an innovative image-based numerical simulation method, release profiles are predicted in a matter of days regardless of the designed release time. A mechanistic understanding on the impact of porosity to the interplays of drug, formulation, process, and dissolution was gained.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder recyclability in metal additive manufacturing has become a critical requirement for improving sustainability, cost-efficiency, and industrial scalability, particularly in powder bed fusion processes such as Selective Laser Melting (SLM) and Electron Beam Melting (EBM). Despite growing interest in powder reuse, the available literature remains fragmented, often addressing powder degradation, process defects, or mechanical performance as isolated topics. This separation limits understanding of how powder lifecycle evolution affects fatigue-critical reliability, where small variations in powder condition may strongly influence long-term structural integrity. This review aims to establish a unified process–structure–performance perspective linking powder reuse, degradation mechanisms, defect evolution, and mechanical reliability in SLM and EBM. A structured literature analysis was conducted to examine changes in powder morphology, particle size distribution, chemical composition, oxygen uptake, moisture interaction, flowability, and thermal history across reuse cycles. Attention was given to the relationship between powder degradation mechanisms and defect formation during processing. The review shows that static mechanical properties, including tensile strength and hardness, may remain comparatively stable after multiple reuse cycles. In contrast, fatigue performance is markedly more sensitive to powder condition, owing to the accumulation of defects such as oxide inclusions, porosity, lack-of-fusion regions, and irregular melt-pool features. Distinct degradation pathways were identified: SLM is mainly governed by oxidation-related effects, whereas EBM is more strongly influenced by particle coarsening, morphology changes, and thermal exposure. Powder recyclability should be considered not only as a sustainability issue but also as a reliability-driven engineering challenge. The proposed framework supports reuse decisions by integrating powder lifecycle assessment with defect tolerance and fatigue-critical performance requirements.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Postural and locomotor dysfunction represent axial symptoms of Parkinson’s disease (PD), which remain poorly treated by medication and deep brain stimulation. Whilst non-invasive neuromodulation of the vestibular system via the vestibular nucleus complex (VNC) offers a novel therapeutic avenue, the underlying circuits are still poorly characterized. Here we show that the mouse VNC feeds extensive
                    <jats:italic>Vglut2</jats:italic>
                    -defined projections into striato-thalamo-subthalamic and caudal medulla motor hubs and receives substantial input from the sensorimotor cortex. Optogenetic activation of excitatory VNC neurons at sub-symptomatic intensities increased
                    <jats:italic>cFos</jats:italic>
                    -based activity in basal ganglia-associated and brainstem motor targets. Unbiased pose dynamics and motion analysis respectively showed enhancement of behavioural modularity and locomotion with threshold-level stimulation. In a mouse model of PD, the latter further favored naturalistic gait patterns through improved motor coordination. Our data identify excitatory VNC processes as candidates for therapeutic targeting of axial motor dysfunction in the context of PD.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
The quality and properties of metal powders are essential for powder metallurgical (PM) processes in general and for additive manufacturing (AM) processing routes in particular. Thus, a variety of atomization technologies were established meeting the multiple needs of the different processing technologies. However, the production of refractory metal alloy powder remains challenging due to their high liquidus temperatures (>2000 °C), the formation of brittle intermetallic phases, as well as the reactivity with and sensitivity to interstitials of the constituting elements. In this contribution, powders made of Mo-20Si-52.8-Ti (at.%) were produced by a novel ultrasonic atomization (UA) process at laboratory-scale using an industrial electrode induction gas atomization (EIGA) process with a modified electrode concept for the first time. UA allows flexibility in alloy composition due to the arc melting-based principle, while the EIGA electrode is PM manufactured from elemental powders to provide similar flexibility on a larger scale. The powders resulting from these two processes were compared with respect to size distribution, sphericity, microstructure and phase constitution, chemical composition, and interstitial impurity content. In addition, several powder batches were produced with the UA process in order to assess the process reliability and stability. The properties, quality, and quantities of UA powders perfectly meet the requests for alloy development for powder bed fusion AM, while the modified EIGA process allows the upscaling of the alloy powder quantities.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Gas atomization is a key technology for producing high-quality metal powders, widely adopted in additive manufacturing and other powder-based industries due to its versatility and productivity. Its complexity, such as intense gas&ndash;liquid momentum exchange, thermal gradients in solidification, and multiple influencing factors, poses significant challenges for process control. This comprehensive review explores the complexities of gas atomization technology in metal powder production, examining the underlying mechanisms, simulation techniques, flow field dynamics, and key influencing factors. It clarifies that primary atomization is characterized by liquid film atomization, driven by Kelvin&ndash;Helmholtz instabilities, and fountain atomization, triggered by Rayleigh&ndash;Taylor instabilities. Secondary atomization, on the other hand, is predominantly influenced by shear and inertial forces. The review emphasizes the key roles of physical gas and liquid properties, temperature, pressure, nozzle design, and solidification processes in determining the characteristics of the resulting metal powder. It concludes that a thorough understanding of these factors is essential for refining the atomization process and improving the quality of the metal powder produced. The review suggests that future research should focus on resolving discrepancies in atomization mechanisms, enhancing simulation methodologies, and investigating the effects of advanced nozzle designs on the production of metal powder.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Copper is a critical material for energy transition and green technologies, making its sustainable use increasingly important. Its superior thermal and electrical conductivity make it highly well-suited for additive manufacturing (AM). In this study, copper sourced from offshore electrical cables was upcycled to produce high-quality metal powder for AM. The scrap was processed to separate the metal from plastic and rubber, then refined through ultrasonic atomization, achieving a purity of ~99.5% wt.% with minimal impurities. Characterization demonstrated good flowability, apparent and tap densities, and a well-distributed particle size. To assess its performance in AM, the powder was printed using Directed Energy Deposition (DED) with a laser beam, confirming its high printability and compatibility with the base material. Finally, a comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) revealed a significant environmental advantage of the recycling-based process over conventional mining, reducing global warming potential by more than 70%. These findings highlight the importance of feedstock origin in AM sustainability and support the adoption of circular economy strategies to lower the environmental footprint of advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Metal powders for additive manufacturing are expensive, and producing new ones from mined metals has a negative ecological impact. In this work, recycled and reused metal powders from MS1 steel for direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) 3D printing were evaluated in the laboratory. The powders were recycled by melting followed by gas atomizing. Virgin, recycled, and reused metal powders were evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), metallography analysis, microhardness measurements, particle size distribution (PSD), shape factor by digital image processing (DIP), and flowability testing. The results showed that the particle distribution was modified after recycling. Kurtosis analysis revealed a reduction from −0.64 for virgin powders to −1.29 for recycled powders. The results demonstrated a positive skewness, indicating that the recycled powder contained a greater proportion of smaller particles. The shape factor was also modified and changed from 1.57 for virgin powders to 1.28 for recycled powders. The microstructure also changed, and austenite was found in the recycled powders. The microhardness of recycled powder decreased by 39% compared to the virgin powder. Recycled powders did not flow, using two different funnels to evaluate their flowability. The flowability of used powder was reduced from 4.3 s to 2.9 s.

Frauke Hinrichs, Alexander Kauffmann, Daniel Schliephake, Sascha Seils, Susanne Obert, Karin Ratschbacher, Melissa Allen, Astrid Pundt, and Martin Heilmaier. Flexible powder production for additive manufacturing of refractory metal-based alloys. Metals, 11:1723, Oct 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met11111723, doi:10.3390/met11111723. This article has 27 citations.

The excerpt provides a qualitative comparison between ultrasonic atomization (UA) and electrode induction gas atomization (EIGA). EIGA powder exhibited satellite particles and irregularly shaped particles, whereas its particle-size range was explicitly described as wider than that of the UA powder. EIGA had a bimodal distribution, with a major peak near 10 µm and a smaller peak around 40 µm; 56% of particles were below 20 µm and 24% were between 40 and 80 µm. Although EIGA particles had slightly higher aspect ratios than UA particles, 90% still had a sphericity better than 1.5, indicating generally good sphericity. The excerpt characterizes UA as having a narrow particle-size distribution, but it does not provide a numerical UA satellite fraction, agglomerate percentage, or a direct quantitative morphology comparison. It likewise does not report typical satellite or agglomerate fractions for either process. Thus, the supplied pages support the conclusion that UA generated a narrower distribution than EIGA, while EIGA contained observable satellites and irregular particles and retained mostly spherical morphology. Additional pages or cited literature would be needed for numerical satellite and agglomerate percentages.

The excerpt directly supports concerns about pixel-resolution bias and consistency in image-based particle measurement. It states that quantitative comparison between laboratories requires standardizing image-generation methods, resolution, and the definitions and formulas used for shape descriptors. Resolution affects basic measurements and shape descriptors: increasing resolution reduces pixel size and generally increases measured perimeter because surface roughness is captured more accurately. Consequently, perimeter-derived measures such as circularity or roundness can vary with resolution even when analyzing the same particle. The authors cite ISO 9276-6 guidance that each particle should occupy approximately 100–5000 pixels to provide adequate precision, particularly for the smallest particles. Higher-resolution SEM imaging may reveal fine morphological features more effectively than optical microscopy, but comparisons remain valid only when imaging and analysis conditions are controlled. The excerpt also emphasizes that different imaging approaches can introduce systematic biases: polished cross sections provide randomized particle orientations, whereas gravity-dispersed shadow projections may preferentially orient particles. These findings are relevant to efforts to improve consistency in particle-size and shape measurement, indicating that resolution, particle representation in pixels, imaging geometry, and descriptor definitions should be documented and harmonized across instruments and laboratories.

The excerpt is relevant to consistency and bias in image-based particle-shape measurement, although it does not mention Mingard or the NPL directly. It compares Clemex and ImageJ methods and shows that software algorithms can produce different perimeter and shape results from the same particle images. Clemex estimates perimeter by interpolating particle-border segments using three points, whereas ImageJ treats horizontal and vertical pixel edges as one unit and diagonal connections as approximately 1.4 units. The MorphoLibJ plug-in applies Crofton’s formula and produces perimeter values 3–5% lower than Clemex, illustrating method-dependent systematic bias. The authors emphasize thresholding as important for obtaining consistent results across systems. Most reported descriptors differed by less than 1%, but convexity was a notable exception: ImageJ values were significantly lower than Clemex values, requiring different classification thresholds (0.90 versus 0.95). Extent ratio, ellipse ratio, and roundness index showed broadly equivalent behavior between systems. The excerpt also notes that ImageJ does not calculate internal and external diameters. Overall, the passage supports the importance of accounting for pixel resolution, diagonal-pixel treatment, threshold selection, perimeter algorithms, and descriptor-specific software bias when improving reproducibility of particle-size and circularity/shape measurements.
